newsitem.title: USA: Fossil prices rise as collectors dig natural history.
newsitem.headline: Fossil prices rise as collectors dig natural history.

text.p: Bones, rocks, teeth and insects were once valued only by museums and scientists seeking clues to the world's prehistory, but no more.
Thanks to a growing interest in the environment, outer space and the blockbuster movie "Jurassic Park," a market for natural history collectibles has emerged among regular Homo sapiens.
Sotheby's is planning a fall sale of the largest Tyrannosaurus Rex fossil ever found, the giant dinosaur whose notoreity in "Jurassic Park" made it a star.
The 45-foot fossil, which includes 90 percent of the creature's bones, is expected to fetch more than $1 million.
On June 21, Phillips Fine Art Auctioneers in New York will hold its bi-annual auction of natural history objects, an event where the value of items sold has steadily surged since 1995.

"There's an increased public awareness of the Earth's history. The more people become aware of something, the more they want to be part of it," said David Herskowitz, a consultant who helped Phillips launch the auction series.
"Owning a T-Rex claw or skull is being part of it. People also buy for the beauty and the 'cool' factor," he said.
For as little as $10 or $20, you can own "cool" jewelry such as pendants or brooches made from a dinosaur bone or a prehistoric insect preserved in amber.

For your mantelpiece or coffee table, a good stingray fossil starts at $1,200, said Eric Kendrew, who owns The Fossil Store, a mail-order catalogue business (813-681-4350). A diplomystus fish, a prehistoric herring, costs $1,000 to $4,000. A fossil of sycamore leaves, whose shape hasn't changed for aeons, is worth $150 to $200.
For deeper pockets, consider a 5-foot-long Triceratops skull. It fetched $74,000 at Phillips last December.
A few years ago, Sotheby's sold a few grains of moon rock brought back by Russian astronauts for $440,000, to a private American buyer. The pre-estimate was only $20,000 to $30,000.
The value depends on the quality and rarity, of course, and how complete a skeleton or other specimen is.
A complete dinosaur tooth that costs $5,000 to $15,000 would be worth only $500 to $5,000 if it were broken.
Many artifacts are bought by amateurs who are fascinated with natural history, rather than by museums or other institutions, which are facing funding problems.
"It's fun to handle something 65 million years old from a great species no one has ever seen," said Henry Galiano, owner of Maxilla and Mandible (212-724-6173), New York's oldest fossil store.
As a result, a Tyrannosaurus tooth that sold for $800 in 1995 was worth $2,000 a year later, he said.

"Thirty years ago, there was no market for it, it didn't sell. It's an upcoming collectible with an investment potential," said Galiano, who worked for the American Museum of Natural History for 15 years.

"Just considering the labour alone in digging and cleaning fossils, it's a good investment. In the future a lot of areas will be off-limits, so fossils will be more rare. In that way they will maintain their value."
But as with any other collectible, prices fluctuate.

A fossilized dinosaur egg that used to cost $3,000 is now worth only $800 to $900 because the demand caused a spurt in imports from China, Galiano said. But the Chinese government has now banned their export, helping to stabilise prices.

While many such eggs were discovered by farmers tilling their fields, don't expect to find any buried prehistoric treasures in your yard -- unless you live in a heavily fossilized area in the Rockies or upstate New York.
Many such areas have now been proclaimed government land, making it illegal for any rocks to be removed. But owners of adjacent land have opened their properties for fossil diggers.

For $35, you can dig all day at Warfield Springs Fossil Quarries in Wyoming (307-883-2445). A hammer and chisel are provided and you can keep your paleontological finds, unless they are rare specimens such as stingrays, birds and turtles.
"All the major discoveries of fossils were made by amateur collectors," said Herskowitz.
To find out about upcoming natural history trade shows call Martin Zen Expositions at 303-674-2713.
